newsitem.title: USA: Pa. Gov. unveils plan to privatize liquor stores.
newsitem.headline: Pa. Gov. unveils plan to privatize liquor stores.

text.p: Pennsylvania Gov. Tom Ridge on Wednesday unveiled a plan to privatize the state's government-run liquor stores, generating hundereds of millions of dollars for state programs.
"Government is here to serve the people, not to serve them alcohol," Ridge said in announcing the plan. "It's time to sell Pennsylvania's state liquor stores."
Pennsylvania is one of only two states that still totally control the retail and wholesale sale of wine and spirits. The other is Utah.

Ridge said his plan, while ending government retail sales, still reflects Pennsylvania's conservative views on alcohol. It would retain tight controls on the availability of alcohol, and step up the penalties for sales to those under age 21.
Ridge said the proceeds of privatization -- estimated to be $605 million over the next 10 years -- should first be used to help state-store employees.
His plan sets aside $20 million for employees, including a $2,000 tax credit for every full-time employee.
Ridge said $57.5 million of the proceeds -- nearly 10 percent of the total -- should be used over the next 10 years to fund enhanced alcohol education and enforcement initiatives.

Of the remaining proceeds 75 percent, or $388 million, would be invested in the Better Communities Fund to build local community projects approved by the state General Assembly, including museums, airports, industrial parks, zoos, theaters and aquariums.

The remaining 25 percent would be invested in new Pennsylvania Community Service Scholarships. The new program would annually award at least 4,000 four-year, $1,000-a-year scholarships to high school seniors in every Pennsylvania graduating class.
Under Ridge's plan the state would retain control of the wholesale system, but close the 654 government wine and spirits stores.

The franchisees would pay up-front fees for their 10-year franchise, and also recurring annual fees. Total proceeds, including proceeds from the ongoing wholesale system, would be $3.2 billion over 10 years, according to Ridge.
